summary: Learners derive and apply the nth-term (position-to-term) rule for an arithmetic sequence, sharply distinguishing it from the term-to-term 'add d' rule. The core structure: the coefficient of n is the common difference, and the constant is the 'zeroth term' one step before the first term (not the first term itself). Fluency means deriving the rule from structure, verifying it by substituting n=1,2,3, jumping to far terms (e.g. the 100th) without listing, and testing membership by solving rule=target and accepting only whole-number positions. Include decreasing and decimal/fraction sequences so the rule generalises.
misconceptions: Uses the common difference as the WHOLE rule: writes n + 4 (or just 'add 4') for 3, 7, 11, 15 instead of 4n − 1
Confuses 'multiples of 3' with 'increases by 3' — assumes a sequence going up by 3 must contain multiples of 3
Whole-object method: finds the 100th term by taking the 10th term × 10, or claims the 10th term is twice the 5th (only true when the line passes through the origin)
Gets the sign wrong for decreasing sequences: writes 4n + 6 for 10, 6, 2, −2 instead of −4n + 14
Attends to the term-to-term rule instead of position, so cannot reach a far term without listing
Over-generalises from only-increasing examples, treating decreasing sequences as a different kind

activities.title: Build the rule from a growing pattern
steps: Work through an illustrative growing shape or matchstick example such as 4, 7, 10, … and rewrite each term to expose structure: 4 = 1+3, 7 = 1+3+3, 10 = 1+3+3+3. Here the fixed start 1 is the zeroth term and the repeated +3 is the coefficient, giving the rule 3n + 1.
Apply the same technique to the target sequence 3, 7, 11, 15: identify the repeated group (+4) as the coefficient of n and the fixed starting part (the zeroth term) as the constant.
Find the zeroth term by stepping back one step before the first term (for 3,7,11,15: 3 − 4 = −1), and state the rule as 4n − 1.
Complete the sentence frame 'As the value of n increases by one, each term increases (or decreases) by ___' and connect that difference to the coefficient of n.
activities.insight: The nth-term rule reads structure directly from position: the coefficient of n IS the common difference, and the constant is the term at position zero — found by stepping back one before the first term, not the first term itself.

activities.title: Position machine: test a rule and jump to far terms
steps: Type a candidate rule into a 'test all' box that substitutes n=1,2,3,4,5 and marks each term green (matches the real sequence) or red (does not).

Watch a wrong rule fail visibly: n+4 turns every cell red (it gives 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 instead of 3, 7, 11, 15, 19), while 4n−1 lights every cell green — so the term-to-term rule and the position rule are seen to differ, not just told apart.
Use a 'jump to n=100' control to produce the 100th term instantly (399 for 4n−1) and feel why listing is absurd.
Repeat the derive-then-verify cycle for a decreasing sequence (10, 6, 2, −2 → −4n + 14) and a decimal/fraction sequence so the rule generalises beyond increasing positive-integer cases.
activities.insight: A position rule can be tested against the real terms and used to leap straight to any position; a rule written as 'n + d' from the term-to-term 'add d' rule generally fails substitution, and the coefficient carries the SIGNED difference, so a decreasing sequence needs a negative coefficient.

activities.title: Membership testing by solving an equation
steps: Given a target number, set the nth-term rule equal to it and solve the linear equation for n.
Accept the target as a term only when n is a whole number; reject it when n is non-integer.
Work the deliberately misleading case: for 3,7,11,15,… test 101 by solving 4n−1 = 101 → 4n = 102 → n = 25.5 → not a whole position → not a term; then test 99 → n = 25 → yes.
When a target is rejected, find the nearest actual terms (99 at n=25 and 103 at n=26) to show which values really belong.
activities.insight: Membership is decided by solving rule=target and checking for a whole-number position, not by whether a number 'looks like' the others (e.g. being odd).

activities.title: Graph the terms and read the difference
steps: Plot the sequence terms against their position numbers.
Read the common difference as the steepness between successive plotted points, and connect this to the coefficient of n.
Do NOT join the points with a line — positions are whole numbers, so non-integer positions have no meaning here.
Use the graph to challenge the whole-object claim: check whether doubling the position doubles the term, and notice this only holds if the plotted line would pass through (0,0).
activities.insight: Steepness on the position-term graph matches the common difference, and multiplying a term's value in step with its position only works when the line passes through the origin.

activities.title: Check and consolidate fluency
steps: Complete fill-the-blank items (e.g. 'nth term of 3,7,11 is __n__') and choose between distractors that pit n+4 against 4n−1.
Answer a multiple-choice item whose distractor is the whole-object claim '100th term = 10th term × 10', explaining why it is wrong.
Decide a membership item where the target (e.g. 101) is odd but not in the sequence, so surface-checking fails and only solving succeeds.
Use a labelled reference card: the sequence with +4 arrows, the rule 4n−1 annotated, and the zeroth term revealed (3−4 = −1) as a consolidation summary after the main work.
activities.insight: Learners can recognise the correct position rule, reject the whole-object shortcut, and settle membership by solving rather than by appearance.

checkQuestion: Here is a sequence: 3, 7, 11, 15, 19, … Find a rule that gives you any term straight from its position number, and use it to work out the 100th term without listing them all. Then tell me: is 101 in this sequence — and how do you know?
checkAnswer: nth term = 4n − 1; 100th term = 399 (4×100 − 1); 101 is NOT a term because 4n − 1 = 101 gives n = 25.5, not a whole-number position (the terms either side are 99 at n=25 and 103 at n=26).
